source.title: Homogenization of SGD in high-dimensions: exact dynamics and generalization properties
source.authors: Courtney Paquette; Elliot Paquette; Ben Adlam; Jeffrey Pennington

record.tranche_reason: The study reports test-risk trajectories over training time for SGD, which bear on epoch-wise double descent, but it does not use the original study’s method or explicitly characterize a fall-rise-fall curve.
record.gate_note: The study measures expected/test risk over training time in Figures 2–4. The plotted values are not given numerically in the text, and the accompanying descriptions do not say whether the trajectories have a fall-rise-fall shape. Figure 1 reports parameter error rather than test error. The discussion of double descent in related work cites other studies and is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: This is a mathematics paper proving that homogenized SGD matches SGD on high-dimensional ℓ2-regularized least squares. Its test-risk-over-time figures (Figs 2–4) exist to show agreement between theory and SGD runs, not to test whether test error falls, rises and falls again. The text never describes any curve as non-monotone or double-descent. Double descent appears only in the titles of cited works (e.g. Belkin et al. 2019, Adlam & Pennington 2020, Mei & Montanari 2022). No model-size, sample-size or noise sweep around an interpolation threshold is run. The results therefore do not bear on any version; the record's 'tests'/T2 is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that homogenized SGD is the high-dimensional equivalent of SGD for quadratic statistics. Its Volterra equations give exact training-loss and risk dynamics and the limiting excess risk of SGD over ridge regression. They draw no conclusion about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes high-dimensional ℓ2-regularized least squares and random-features SGD using homogenized-SGD theory and Volterra equations; it does not reproduce a double-descent size or sample sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported test-risk trajectories vary with learning rate in the MNIST experiment; Figure 4 discusses the tradeoff between learning rate and speed/noise.
record.problems: The test-risk curve values are only presented in figures, and the text does not characterize their shapes. The SGD comparisons include small numbers of runs in some examples, including one SGD run for Figure 2.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 parameter-error trajectories were excluded because parameter error is not test error. Figure 3's Volterra predictions were excluded as theoretical comparators rather than model outcomes. Other cited double-descent results were not included because they are from prior work.

untested.parts: Risk-over-time curves are shown only to validate the theory; no claim or analysis of a non-monotone epoch-wise curve.
No isolated increase in sample count near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep past an interpolation point.
No effective-complexity measure of peak location.
No noise or regularization dependence of a peak.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'tests' (T2) to cites_only/T6. The only double-descent content is in the titles of cited papers, including original source Belkin et al. 2019. All nine rows relinked to 'none'.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep testing test error around an interpolation threshold.
Reports test-risk trajectories over training time, but does not explicitly test or describe a fall-rise-fall shape.
No isolated increase in training sample count near an interpolation threshold; the cited varying-n setup also varies dimension.
No capacity sweep across model classes testing risk past an interpolation point.
No test of whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across axes.
No test of peak dependence on label noise or regularization, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization removing a peak.
No test of whether an effective parameter count turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
